title: The Uniform of Manchester's mill district
premise: In 1917 Manchester, Wendell Winterbourne works as a battlefield nurse turned convalescent-ward orderly, secretly recording in his ledger the names of common soldiers that officers' reports omit. When a stranger arrives bearing letters in the handwriting of Captain Edmund Ashworth—officially dead at Passchendaele and Wendell's estranged half-brother through their father's hidden second family—Wendell learns Edmund faked his death to escape court-martial and is hiding among the mill workers. As a troop ship's final medical berth becomes available and military police close in, Wendell must decide whether to expose Edmund to save his own reputation, or surrender the berth—and the truth of their father's bigamy—to the brother who once abandoned him. He chooses truth over loyalty: he gives Edmund the berth but publishes the ledger, ending in disgrace yet finally visible under his own name.
about_author: Freya Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing First World War hospital records in northern England. Her fiction is known for excavating the quiet lives history filed away.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In the Manchester convalescent ward, Wendell tends wounded mill workers while privately recording names officers omit from official reports. The emotional beat is quiet vigilance: we see a man who has made invisibility his craft, tending bodies and paper trails with equal care, haunted by a name he refuses to write down—his own.

chapters.title: A Stranger with Familiar Ink
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A gaunt stranger arrives asking after 'the man who keeps lists,' carrying letters in handwriting Wendell knows intimately: his half-brother Edmund's, officially killed at Passchendaele. The beat is vertigo—the past arriving in daylight. Wendell realizes his careful anonymity has been seen through by someone who shares his blood and his father's secrets.

chapters.title: What Father Buried Twice
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with flashback. Through the stranger's testimony, Wendell reconstructs his father's double life: two families, one mill fortune, and Edmund raised as heir while Wendell was raised as error. The emotional beat is old grief sharpened into new anger—he understands now why Edmund's 'death' felt like theft even before it was a lie.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Ward matron's POV. A single medical berth on the last hospital ship home is allotted to the ward, and Matron tasks Wendell with selecting the recipient. The beat is mounting pressure: every patient has a claim, and Wendell alone knows the berth could also buy Edmund's escape from the military police closing on the district.

chapters.title: Mill Smoke and False Names
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Hiding as a fitter in the Ashworth mills, Edmund navigates the workers' suspicion and the approaching detectives, reading his own obituary pinned to a noticeboard. The beat is corrosive guilt: he watches Wendell's ledger names posted by grieving families and understands what his brother has been carrying for him all along.

chapters.title: An Officer's Silence
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Major Calloway, who suspects Wendell's ledger, offers protection in exchange for testimony against the deserter believed to be alive. The beat is temptation and dread: exposing Edmund would restore Wendell's standing and bury the scandal of their father—but would betray the only person who knows what those omissions cost.

chapters.title: The Night Ward
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. During an air-raid blackout, brothers meet face to face for the first time in fifteen years, among patients too injured to notice. The beat is raw confrontation: accusations about the will, the mother, the name—until Edmund admits he faked his death not for cowardice but because he was the witness his father needed silenced.

chapters.title: Which Name Gets Saved
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. With police sweeping the mills and the ship sailing at dawn, Wendell must choose the berth's recipient between Private Hollis, a dying mill lad whose name exists only in his ledger, and Edmund. The beat is agonizing deliberation—loyalty to the voiceless many against loyalty to the one blood tie he has left.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, then Wendell's. At the dockside, Wendell gives the berth to Hollis and instead hands Edmund his own discharge papers and identity—a sacrifice that makes Wendell legally invisible so his brother can be visibly saved. The beat is reversal: the keeper of others' names surrenders his own, as Calloway arrives with arrest warrants.

chapters.title: Published Under My Own Name
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Disgraced but free, Wendell submits the full ledger to the press, naming every omitted soldier—including Edmund Ashworth, living. The beat is hard-won resolution: truth costs him career and cover, but standing in the mill district where workers now speak the names aloud, Wendell is finally, irreversibly seen.
